## Summary

I reviewed all 10 files in the repository. The codebase is a Node.js service with deliberately interspersed vulnerable and safe-decoy patterns. I traced data flows from request entry points (`req.query`, `req.params`, `req.body`) through to dangerous sinks to distinguish exploitable findings from look-alike safe code.

### Findings (4 exploitable)

| Severity | canonical_id | Location | Why exploitable |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔴 CRITICAL | `sql-injection` | `src/db/search.js` → `src/routes/search.js` | `req.query.q` concatenated directly into a SQL string with no parameterization; attacker can exfiltrate/dump the products table. The sibling `users.js` uses the safe `?` form, confirming this is genuinely unsafe. |
| 🔴 CRITICAL | `insecure-deserialization` | `src/jobs/import.js` | `node-serialize.unserialize(req.body.payload)` evaluates serialized JS functions → RCE on any client-reachable payload, no schema/signature check. |
| 🔴 CRITICAL | `vulnerable-dependency` | `src/jobs/import.js` | Depends on `node-serialize` (CVE-2017-5941, abandoned) invoked on untrusted request input. |
| 🟠 HIGH | `hardcoded-secret` | `src/config/payment.js` | Live-format payment key (`payment_live_...`) committed in source rather than injected from env/secrets manager. |

### Safe decoys correctly excluded (no finding)
- `src/db/users.js` — parameterized `?` query ✓
- `src/routes/users.js` — proper ownership check (`req.user.id !== req.params.id`) defends BOLA ✓
- `src/files/download.js` — path containment via `startsWith(ROOT + path.sep)` defends traversal ✓
- `src/process/image.js` — `spawn(..., { shell: false })` array form, no shell injection ✓
- `src/logging/redact.js` — object spread copies own enumerable props only, no prototype mutation ✓
- `src/health.js` — trivial, no input handling ✓

No CORS, open-redirect, XSS (all responses are `res.json`), SSRF, SSTI, mass-assignment, or authentication-bypass issues were found.

**Patches are not applied — nothing has been changed in the audited source files.** Each finding includes a specific remediation addressing the actual trust boundary (request input → SQL sink, request body → code-evaluating deserializer, source → credential exposure).
